title: Title, date and occasion
short: A 'nocturnal' is a night office or night-piece; St Lucy's Day, 13 December, was the shortest day under the old Julian calendar.
body: A nocturn was a division of the night office of prayer, so the title promises a liturgy for the darkest hour. Under the Julian calendar, still used in England in Donne's day, 13 December was reckoned the shortest day of the year: hence 'the shortest day'. The poem was first printed in 1633 and cannot be securely dated. Grierson was inclined to connect it with Lucy, Countess of Bedford, Donne's patron, perhaps in the year of her serious illness, 1612, while allowing that it 'might have been written to Ann More', the woman Donne married and who died in August 1617. Gosse, whom Grierson quotes, thought the lady's death 'assumed, not actual'. Other readers have taken the poem as a response to Anne Donne's death, which is possible but unproved. The 'shee' of the poem is never named, and many readers treat the death as at least partly imagined.

title: Lucy unmasks
short: St Lucy, whose name comes from Latin lux, light, shows her face (the daylight) for barely seven hours.
body: Lucy of Syracuse, a virgin martyr of c. 304, was traditionally a saint of light and of eyes, her name being derived from Latin lux. Donne makes the saint a masked lady at a court entertainment who 'unmaskes' only briefly: the December day is a face uncovered for less than seven hours. The pun on the name also points toward the Lucy of the poem's occasion (whether the Countess of Bedford or another), so that the shortness of the saint's day mirrors the absence of the poet's light. The day is personified as 'shee', anticipating the dead woman of the last stanza whose 'long nights festivall' replaces her day.

title: flasks ... light squibs
short: The exhausted sun gives off only feeble flashes, like cheap fireworks, instead of steady beams.
body: Endicott glosses 'flasks' as an obsolete form of 'flashes'; it may also keep the sense of powder-flasks, the containers of a gunner's powder, since 'squibs' were small fireworks or crackers that fizz and go out. The sun, 'spent' like a used-up charge, can manage only spurts of light, 'no constant rayes'. The image belongs to Donne's world of contemporary objects: the cosmic decline of the solstice is pictured as a firework display petering out. Compare 'A flaske of powder burne a day' in Donne's 'The Broken Heart', where Grierson defends 'flaske' against the 'flash' of later editions.

title: The general balm
short: The life-preserving balsam believed to be present in all things has been drained away, swallowed by the thirsty earth.
body: Renaissance physiology held that every living body contains a natural balsam, an innate preservative that keeps it fresh and wards off decay; Endicott cites Donne's verse letter to the Countess of Bedford, 'In every thing there naturally grows / A Balsamum to keep it fresh and new', and Grierson prints the sermon passages on the 'naturall Balsamum' that lie behind it. At the solstice the 'worlds whole sap is sunke': the vital moisture of nature has gone down into the ground. The stanza assembles a picture of a dying world, its sap, balm and light all withdrawn, only to say in its final line that all these 'seeme to laugh' compared with the speaker.

title: hydroptique
short: Dropsical: the earth is like a patient with dropsy, whose disease brings an insatiable thirst.
body: 'Hydroptic' (from Greek hydrops, dropsy) describes a sufferer from dropsy, the accumulation of fluid in the body, a disease traditionally said to produce a thirst that drinking only increases. The earth, swollen yet still thirsty, has drunk up the world's balm. Donne liked the figure: the dropsy of insatiable desire recurs elsewhere in his work. The medical register continues in the next line with the patient shrunk to the foot of the bed.

title: as to the beds-feet life is shrunke
short: Life has withdrawn to the foot of the bed, as a dying patient slides down towards it.
body: Helen Gardner, cited by Endicott, traced the image to Hippocrates' signs of approaching death: a patient who sinks down to the foot of the bed shows a 'still more dangerous symptom' (Adams's translation of the Prognostics). Life in the world has contracted into the earth's lowest part, as warmth retreats from a dying body. The next line adds 'Dead and enterr'd', the vocabulary of the burial service, preparing for the speaker's claim that he is their 'Epitaph'.

title: who am their Epitaph
short: The speaker is not merely dead like the world, but the inscription that sums up and records its death.
body: An epitaph is the inscription on a tomb. All the dead things of the first stanza seem cheerful beside the speaker, who is the very summary of their deadness, written over them. The conceit turns him from a person into a sign, preparing for the next stanza's invitation to 'Study me', as one would read a text. The stanza's movement, from the year's midnight down to the single figure of the speaker, is typical of the poem's narrowing focus.

title: Study me then, you who shall lovers bee
short: Future lovers, those of 'the next world', which is merely next spring, should study him as a lesson in love's power to annihilate.
body: The address to lovers recalls the advice-to-lovers convention of 'The Canonization', where the saints of love become a 'patterne' for others. Here the speaker offers himself as a negative example. The 'next world' is wittily deflated into 'the next Spring', the season of renewed lovemaking that the solstice promises everyone except him; the final stanza returns to these lovers with the sun's journey to the Goat.

title: every dead thing
short: The 1633 text reads 'every'; later editions read 'very'. Grierson kept 'every': the speaker is the essence of all dead things.
body: The editions of 1635 to 1669 print 'For I am a very dead thing' or similar; 1633 and some manuscripts read 'every'. Grierson kept 'every' as the harder and more meaningful reading: the speaker is the quintessence of all negations, 'absence, darknesse, death; things which are not', and finally of 'the first nothing'. 'Very' would make the line merely emphatic. Most modern editors follow 1633. The phrase sets up the alchemical conceit of the stanza, in which love distils a quintessence from nothing.

title: love wrought new Alchimie ... A quintessence
greek: Latin quinta essentia (fifth essence); Arabic al-kimiya
short: Love is an alchemist who, reversing the usual process, extracts a quintessence from nothingness rather than from matter.
body: Alchemy sought to distil from base matter the quintessence, the 'fifth essence' beyond the four elements, thought to be latent in all things and to compose the heavenly bodies. 'Expresse' means to press out. Love's 'new' alchemy works on 'dull privations' and 'leane emptinesse', producing the quintessence of nothing. Grierson discusses the stanza's punctuation at length: following the 1719 text, the 'privations' and 'emptinesse' expand 'nothingnesse'; with the earlier pointing, 'From dull privations' would go with 'He ruin'd mee'. He calls the passage difficult in a difficult poem.

title: ruin'd ... re-begot
short: Love reduced him to his elements and then re-created him out of absence, darkness and death.
body: Endicott suggests that 'ruin'd' is used in an alchemical sense, the reduction of a substance to its elements before it is transformed, and that 'absence, darknesse, death' probably correspond to the three alchemical principles, salt, sulphur and mercury. The speaker is then 're-begot', reborn, but his new parents are negations. The line ends on 'things which are not', which may echo 1 Corinthians 1:28, where God chooses 'things which are not, to bring to nought things that are'.

title: loves limbecke
short: A limbeck (alembic) is a distilling vessel; love's still has made him the grave of everything that is nothing.
body: The limbeck, or alembic, is the cap of a still in which vapours condense, a standard piece of alchemical apparatus. Where 'all others' draw life, soul, form and spirit from things, the speaker, distilled by love, is 'the grave / Of all, that's nothing': he receives only negation. The word continues the alchemy of the second stanza and prepares for the 'Elixer' of the fourth.

title: flood ... two Chaosses ... carcasses
short: Recalling their love, he says their tears drowned their world, their distractions reduced them to chaos, and absences made them corpses.
body: Stanza three remembers the lovers' past as a series of small apocalypses. Their weeping was a Flood that 'Drownd the whole world, us two' (lovers as a world is a favourite Donne idea, as in 'The Good-morrow'); when they cared for anything else, each became a 'Chaos', the formless matter before creation; and absences 'Withdrew our soules', leaving 'carcasses', since the soul of each lover lay in the other. These negations prepare for the stanza that follows, in which her death reduces him to something below even chaos: 'the first nothing'.

title: (which word wrongs her)
short: The parenthesis objects that 'death' is the wrong word for her, perhaps because she is now in bliss, or because the speaker cannot accept it.
body: The first explicit mention of her death comes with a correction. Readers take the aside in different ways: as a Christian reservation (she is not dead but translated to a higher life, which the last stanza's 'festivall' and 'Vigill' support), as a lover's refusal to apply a common word to her, or as a sign that the death is a poetic hypothesis rather than fact, which was Gosse's view, reported by Grierson. The parenthesis interrupts the line exactly as the event interrupts the poem.

title: the first nothing, the Elixer
short: Her death makes him the elixir, the pure essence, of the nothing that preceded God's creation.
body: 'Elixir' here means quintessence, as Grierson shows from the OED. The 'first nothing' is the void from which God created the world (creation ex nihilo). Donne wrote in his Essays in Divinity that this nothing was 'no creature' and so more incomprehensible than anything created, a passage Grierson quotes. The poem, he observes, turns on degrees of nothingness: love made the speaker nothing, but her death makes him the essence of the absolute nothing before creation, below even chaos (stanza 3), which was at least matter.

title: man ... beast ... plants, yea stones
short: Running down the scale of being, he says that men, beasts, plants and even stones have some likes and dislikes; he has none.
body: The lines rehearse the Aristotelian and scholastic hierarchy of souls. A man, with a rational soul, would know his preferences; a beast, with a sensitive soul, would choose ends and means; plants, with a vegetative soul, take what nourishes and reject what does not; even stones attract and repel. Grierson quotes a sermon in which Donne allows that stones may have life. Since the speaker has no such properties, he is below the whole chain. Grierson also rejects the Grolier Club punctuation of ll. 31-2 as unintelligible.

title: an ordinary nothing ... As shadow
short: Even a shadow, an everyday 'nothing', needs a light and a body to exist; he lacks both, because his sun has gone.
body: A shadow is a negation, yet it implies the presence of light and of a body to block it. Grierson quotes a sermon in which Donne argues that if there is no shadow when the sun shines, there is no body in that place either. The speaker is not even an 'ordinary nothing': with his light, the woman, gone, he cannot cast a shadow. The thought leads straight into 'But I am None', the poem's lowest point.

title: my Sunne ... the lesser Sunne
short: The woman is his sun, which will not return; the literal sun is merely the 'lesser' one.
body: 'But I am None' may carry a pun on Donne's own name, as his poems often do (compare 'A Hymne to God the Father', which plays on 'Done'). His private sun, the woman, will not renew itself as the solar sun does after the solstice. Calling the real sun 'the lesser Sunne' inverts the order of the cosmos for love's sake, a move familiar from 'The Sunne Rising'. Some readers also hear the Christian Son behind 'Sunne', since the poem ends with a vigil.

title: the Goat
short: At the winter solstice the sun enters Capricorn, the Goat, a beast proverbial for lust.
body: The sun enters the zodiacal sign of Capricorn (the goat) at the winter solstice. Because the goat was the emblem of lechery, Donne imagines the sun travelling there 'to fetch new lust' for the lovers of the coming spring. The astronomical fact becomes an erotic errand from which the speaker is excluded: 'Enjoy your summer all'. Grierson argues that the full stop after 'Enjoy your summer all' (l. 41) is right, so that the following clause ('Since shee enjoyes...') explains the speaker's preparation, not the lovers' summer.

title: her Vigill, and her eve
short: A vigil is the night watch before a saint's feast; he will keep this hour as the eve of her festival.
body: In the church calendar a vigil, or eve, is the night of prayer before a feast day. The speaker turns St Lucy's night into the vigil of the dead woman, whose 'long nights festivall' is her death, or her new life. He means to 'prepare towards her', that is, toward his own death and reunion. The religious vocabulary implicitly canonizes her, making her a second Lucy, and gives the poem its character as a 'nocturnal', a night office.

title: Stanza form and circular close
short: The last line returns to the first: the poem begins and ends at the midnight of both year and day.
body: Each of the five nine-line stanzas rhymes abbacccdd and mixes line lengths, with shorter lines in the middle of each stanza that seem to contract, like the light. The final line echoes the opening, 'Tis the yeares midnight, and it is the dayes', so that the poem enacts a single unmoving hour. The circular structure has been read as a sign that no progress or consolation is possible within the poem, though the vigil looks beyond it.
